body_markdown:
The Hagerty Against All Oddities fandom and community is alive. Growing. A couple of months back, something amazing happened: One of you reached out and offered us, the car commune known as the Troutman Foundry, a car. A whole Plymouth Fury! I had promised to curb our fleet’s numbers, but alas, sometimes opportunity knocks. How could I say no to a free, white whale of a station wagon that someone else had given up on? It would be bad manners to reject such a thing.


So how did this all start? A guy by the name of Ruffin reached out to Hagerty Media with a kind offer:


> *“I recalled an Against All Oddities from this January where \[Matt\] mentioned…*
>
>
> ‘ ***At the shop, we brainstormed different ideas. Maybe it was time for a 318 (Chrysler LA engine) or a 5.2 Magnum swap for old Fuggles \[the broken Dodge shop truck\]? Thomas had a line on a $300 318 from a Plymouth Fury.*** ‘
>
>
> *Well, I’ve got a 1972 Plymouth Fury wagon that I’m pretty sure has a 318 that’s been in my yard for over a decade that I finally figured I’d never get around to fixing up. It ran the last time I tried… which was probably in 2004.*
>
>
> *I’m also in Charleston, SC. \[Given your mentions of\] the Hickory Sweeper (a half-hour away?), I-77, and trips to Virginia & Fort Mill, I’m guessing you’re near the hornet’s nest in NC. So we’re close.*
>
>
> *I can’t decide if anyone would be interested in this thing or if I need to scrap it. It’s mostly trashed out. Still goes in and out of gear. (Ask how I know. Thanks, county code enforcement.)*
>
>
> *If you promise to at least try to do something with some part of it beyond scrapping it (or at least have it outside your shop for a year or more thinking you might), you can come take some or all of it.”*
>
>
> [Matthew Anderson](https://www.hagerty.com/media/author/manderson/)
>
>
> What other option did I have than to say YES?!


A 1972 Plymouth Fury Suburban is a pretty convenient storage container for a 318. Fuggles the Dodge Shop Truck is long gone, but regardless, it seemed the logical thing to gratefully accept the offer and make a plan later. Visions popped into my head of a Troutman Foundry logo on the driver and passenger doors, the car lowered slightly and sitting on some Keystone Klassics. (With thin whitewalls, of course.) Furthermore, the idea of a car with some amount of domestic parts availability[sounds extremely attractive right now](https://www.hagerty.com/media/opinion/against-all-oddities/against-all-oddities-vive-la-simca/) . Sure, what the heck?


Ruffin and I corresponded for several weeks, but my work travel schedule kept me from getting down to the car’s location in Charleston. Plan A was to make this a family vacation, tacking the Fury retrieval onto the tail end of the trip. Now that my son August is a toddler, we have a little more flexibility in planning these sorts of things. Plus, my wife is a saint. Even so, there were appreciable risks to badging this as a family vacation, even if it was going to involve two days of us enjoying the city and eating seafood. A third day of catastrophic sh**box retrieval could undo all of that goodwill.


Troutman Foundry fall catalog.


[Matthew Anderson](https://www.hagerty.com/media/author/manderson/)


Enter dockhands Thomas and Dekoven. Even though they were already planning to leave for Ohio on a Midwest car museum tour, they agreed to do the Fury grab and set off for South Carolina on a Tuesday afternoon. The deal would work as follows: take the Tundra shop truck and a trailer down on Tuesday night, stay with friend (and Simca half-owner) Connor in downtown Charleston, and I’d buy them all a good meal at my old local haunt, Moe’s Crosstown Tavern. Obviously, I’d pay for gas and supplies, and Thomas would log working hours like the real trucker he is.


The guys got down early enough to check out some of Connor’s car collection (a W124 Mercedes 500E and a Citroën 2CV were on site) and then headed to Moe’s. (I recommend the goat cheese and poblano burger.) The following morning, they headed out to Ruffin’s place in Mount Pleasant, just over the bridge and into the jungle. They found the car there in a clearing, exactly where Ruffin had dropped the pin on the map. I was jealous of the treasure hunt, and I followed along while at my day job, via text thread from a seat at the dyno in California.


Thomas had brought along a large battery and some starter fluid to see if they could get the car driving onto the trailer. According to Ruffin, it had run a short 22 years ago. After dumping some gas down the carb and throwing in the new battery, it lit off. Thomas reported that it was “hitting on all seven,” on account of squirrels having eaten one of the plug wires. All were amused by the Carter BBD carburetor, which was a pleasant surprise. Also of note: When these Furites came with the 318, they also got the small-pattern bellhousing for the 727, which matches that of a Gen III Hemi. Coworker, friend, and fellow C-body owner Nelson has donated a set of engine mounts. Hmm… possibilities.


To everyone’s surprise, the Fury ran and moved under its own power. Its pedal functions were limited to forward motion, though, as the brakes were completely out, parking brake included, so it still had to be towed up onto the trailer. On initial inspection, things looked exactly as advertised. Three cheers for the shop car! And even more cheers for Ruffin!


Looking for more squirrels.


[Matthew Anderson](https://www.hagerty.com/media/author/manderson/)


The ride home was allegedly buttery smooth and made me happy to have our 320,000-mile shop truck on hand. When unloading back at the foundry after a very long day, the guys forgot that the car had zero stopping ability, and it came to a draw between the rear quarter panel and the old crucible lying in the yard. Not how I would have preferred the unloading to go, but the car is far from perfect, and backing into a crucible is now simply part of its story. Can’t be too mad about it, especially if it makes the Troutman Foundry logos a bit more legit.


So now what? Well, there’s no title. It’s an old Georgia car on a bill of sale, so I have a bit of paperwork to do. I’m also thinking of making this a shop parts hauler. Given the parts availability, it seems like a no-brainer to stock up on what we need, order a whole bunch of pizzas, and throw a recommissioning party. Do they sell tetanus shots in 24-packs?


Out with the old.


[Matthew Anderson](https://www.hagerty.com/media/author/manderson/)


I must give a big, hearty thank-you to Ruffin for his generosity and flexibility. A big plus: The car didn’t go directly to the crusher, and following the initial inspection, it seems unlikely it will anytime soon. After the pickup, he sent this note along:


> *Tell you what, Thomas knows his C-bodies. Instantly knew more about my Fury than I ever did* … *they got it moving pretty quickly.*
>
>
> *Thomas promised he’d, worst case, get at least a one wheel burnout out of it, maybe practice some rust repair, and I should watch the shop’s Instagram. That’s a whole lot more interesting than selling it to the scrapper. Maybe a Fury wagon lover will catch wind of it in Statesville and you can make them a deal.*
>
>
> *Lemme know when the beer garden is up at the Foundry. Until then, I’m off to check YouTube to see how BBDs work… Enjoy your travels.*
>
>
> What an amazing thing to have happened. It’s a win-win-win. Ruffin won’t go to Mt. Pleasant code enforcement jail, a vintage Plymouth lives another day, and the foundry gains a new project.
>
>
> What a community. Against All Oddities forever!


It’s alive!
